input.rationale: Narrows the trim child's open gap with a source reading of the leader's recorded-accepted bookkeeping, so that the remaining part of that question is only the storage-level entry point rather than the whole route. No execution was requested and nothing was run: reading LeaderState::get_min_all_accepted_idx (util.rs 186-191) shows the bound is the minimum over an accepted_indexes vector that the source asserts is initialised for every node (its expect message is Should be all initialised to 0), and set_promise rewrites the promise entry for the sender on every promise. A node therefore has a recorded accepted index from the start, and trim can pass a live replica's accepted index only when that replica's own recorded value has itself been inflated by the re-synchronization drift. That closes, by source, the sub-route the gap named as a peer compacted while its recorded values were still truthful: the trim bound cannot exceed a truthful peer's accepted index, because the truthful peer's own record keeps the minimum honest. What remains of the gap is the storage-level entry point - a direct range read or a store-level trim below a compacted index, which the Storage trait leaves to the implementer and which no run exercised - and the answer records that split explicitly, keeping the gap unresolved while marking the in-cluster half closed. The account's conclusion, witness, controls and knowledge uses are unchanged, and the trimmed trim-bound fact now carries the initialisation evidence in its own conditions in the same update.

knowledge.statement: Trim's bound is the minimum of the leader's recorded accepted indexes and both trim paths respect it: with no explicit index that minimum is used, and an explicit index above it is refused with that same minimum reported. The bound can therefore exceed only the content of replicas whose recorded accepted index has itself drifted; a replica whose report is still truthful keeps the bound at or below its own accepted index, so no in-cluster re-synchronization request can fall below a compacted index that trim produced.
knowledge.conditions: Leader role, reached from the public trim() with None or Some(index). The minimum is taken over the leader's accepted_indexes vector, which the source asserts is initialised for every node (get_min_all_accepted_idx at util.rs 186-191 returns the vector's minimum and its expect message reads Should be all initialised to 0), and set_promise rewrites the entry for the promising node, so every configuration member has a recorded value even if it has never sent an Accepted message. Witnessed in receipt ec3329dc273e452aa92bcd44652c116a (recorded values 10, 9 and 7 over six indices of content, compacted 7, events 9-15). The unexecuted remainder is a storage or caller that asks the storage trait directly for a prefix below the compacted index, whose behaviour the trait leaves to the implementer.
knowledge.changed_premise: Adds the basis for the in-cluster half of the claim rather than leaving it as an inference from the drift: the minimum is taken over a per-node vector the source says is initialised for every member, so a truthful replica keeps the bound at or below its own accepted index and no re-synchronization request can fall below a trim-produced compacted index. Previously the statement asserted the same consequence from the observed drift alone.

interpretations.rationale: Witnessed and bounded, with the second producer recorded and with the suffix route split into an executed in-cluster half and an unexecuted storage-level half. The trim witness stands: with recorded accepted indexes drifted to 10, 9 and 7 over six indices of content and every node's decided report at 9, trim(None) returned no error and compacted index 7, past the leader's own content, after which its reads of indices 5 and 6 reported Trimmed (ec3329dc273e452aa92bcd44652c116a events 9-15). The discriminator this question carried asked whether a producer other than trim can raise a compacted index past a replica's content, and the snapshot receipt answers that it can: with the same drifted state, snapshot(Some(8), false) returned Ok, advanced the leader's compacted index to 8 and produced a snapshot holding none of the five decided entries (e70b8baa087246c78ea3a64f24b8e97c events 0-5). That second producer is stricter in one respect and looser in another than trim: it needs no recorded accepted index at all - its bound is the leader's decided index - so a drift confined to the decided index would be enough for it, while trim additionally needs the drifted value to be the configuration's minimum recorded accepted index. What remains bounded from the earlier reading: both producers are bounded by values the leader derives for itself, so a replica whose recorded report is still truthful keeps trim's bound honest (the minimum), and the snapshot witness also required the leader's own decided index to have drifted. Correction review: the drift knowledge this account cites was narrowed to revision 2, which keeps the half this account needs - the reported accepted index drifts one further index per re-synchronization round, inflating exactly the recorded accepted indexes the trim bound is derived from - and bounds the decided index to the rounds in which a write quorum of drifted reports covers it; this account never assumes the decided index keeps following the drift, since it reads the decided values from its own receipt's samples (every node at 9), so the narrowing leaves its conclusion unchanged and the knowledge use is re-read at revision 2 below. The suffix route is now split by source and by execution. Executed in-cluster: in the snapshot-capable sibling case the lagging replica re-synchronized below the leader's compacted index (the leader had compacted to 8 with a snapshot holding zero ids) was not refused and did not panic - it received that complete snapshot and no suffix, reported accepted 10 / decided 10 and read two decided entries where the configuration decided six (0b9c22ae5fb043588aa7efa3ad009b25 events 152-162). Closed by source: a re-synchronization request below a trim-produced compacted index cannot arise inside the cluster, because the trim bound is the minimum over the leader's accepted_indexes vector and that vector carries an entry for every configuration member from the start (get_min_all_accepted_idx at util.rs 186-191 returns the vector's minimum and its expect message reads Should be all initialised to 0, while set_promise rewrites the sender's entry on every promise). A replica that has never been inflated therefore keeps its own accepted index in the minimum and trim cannot pass it; only inflation of that replica's own recorded value moves the bound, which is what the witness shows. What is left of the gap is the storage-level entry point: a direct range read or a store-level trim below a compacted index, whose behaviour the Storage trait leaves to the implementer and which no execution exercised, and the abort that this lineage did produce comes from a different entry point, the public snapshot call on a NoSnapshot instance (40ab66a5c5c847619ae2ff68b85641e7-question-1).

b26c13954e184cd2b9fdfda975aff136-gap-4.explanation: Split into a closed in-cluster half and an open storage-level half, so the gap stays unresolved. Closed by source and execution: a replica re-synchronizing below a compacted index does not panic - it is handed a complete snapshot built from the empty part of the log and a shortened decided log (receipt 0b9c22ae5fb043588aa7efa3ad009b25 events 152-162, guarded result event 162 with panicked false) - and a request below a trim-produced compacted index cannot arise inside the cluster at all, because the trim bound is the minimum of the leader's recorded accepted indexes and that per-node vector is initialised for every member (get_min_all_accepted_idx, util.rs 186-191, whose expect message reads Should be all initialised to 0), so a truthful replica keeps the bound at or below its own accepted index and only its own inflation can move it. Still open: the storage-level routes the gap names - a direct range read and a store-level trim below a compacted index - which the Storage trait leaves to the implementer and which no run exercised; and a forwarded Compaction::Snapshot arriving at a NoSnapshot instance, which cannot be produced inside a cluster whose nodes share one entry type because the sender panics first.

ebbec352695d43beb398bb1b239cda41-gap-6.explanation: The narrowed knowledge retains the drift of the reported accepted index, which is the half this account relies on: the trim bound is the minimum of the recorded accepted indexes, so what matters here is that each re-synchronization raises the reported accepted index by one index over unchanged content, and the account reads the decided values from its own receipt's samples rather than from the assumption that the decided index keeps following the drift. The conclusion, the witness and the content comparison are therefore unchanged; the knowledge use is re-read at revision 2.

ebbec352695d43beb398bb1b239cda41-gap-8.explanation: Same review as the sibling note for this knowledge revision: this account uses the drift of the reported accepted index (the trim bound's input) and its own sampled decided values, not the unbounded following of the decided index that the correction narrowed, so the correction does not change the conclusion or the witness, and the knowledge use is re-read at revision 2.

limitations: The trim over-compaction is bounded to replicas whose recorded accepted index has drifted; a truthful replica would have kept the bound lower, and the per-node initialisation of the recorded vector is the reason.

The underflow remainder is a property of a storage or caller that requests a prefix below the compacted index by a route other than the cluster's own log syncs: a direct range read and a store-level trim below a compacted index remain unexecuted, other storage implementations may differ, and the trait leaves out-of-range behaviour to the implementer. The abort observed in this lineage came from the NoSnapshot snapshot-call path, not from this remainder.
The baseline comparisons of both receipts are unknown because they were admitted through event names shared across cases in one execution; those states are asserted from the sampled operands.

One three-node configuration, three reconnection rounds, one leader change for trim and one snapshot-capable entry type were exercised; the peers that receive a forwarded compaction were not sampled beyond their accepted and decided indexes, and the lagging-replica outcome was observed with the leader's log empty above its compacted index.

For the trim path the observed over-compaction is the minimum of the drifted recorded values, so the number of indices it passes beyond the leader's content depends on how many rounds each replica drifted; only one such combination was sampled.

The initialisation claim for the recorded accepted vector is read from the source's own expect message and from set_promise rewriting the sender's entry; no execution sampled the vector directly or ran a trim while one member had never promised.

knowledge.statement: InternalStorage::sync_log sets accepted_idx = LogSync.sync_idx + LogSync.suffix.len() and, when LogSync.stopsign is Some, adds one further index for that StopSign before returning; it does not subtract the LogSync's prefix, so when sync_idx already addresses the StopSign's own index the replica's accepted index ends up one larger than the entries it holds, and each further re-synchronization of the same replica adds one more index while its content is unchanged. SequencePaxos::create_log_sync does not adjust sync_idx for a StopSign already present on the sender: it uses its caller's common_prefix_idx unchanged and attaches the sender's stored StopSign.

knowledge.statement: A leader in the accept phase accepts a decision at the accepted index reported by any matching-ballot Accepted message: it records that index for the sender, and if the index exceeds its own decided index and a write quorum of recorded accepted indexes covers it, it sets its decided index to exactly that reported index, without comparing it against the length of its own log or against its own accepted index.

knowledge.statement: When a candidate becomes leader it adopts two independently ordered inputs in one call: the log comes from the promise that is strictly greatest under (n_accepted, accepted_idx) with pid only as tiebreak, while the decided index is the maximum decided index over all recorded promises; sync_log then writes that decided index and the adopted log in the same storage transaction, and the leader path contains no clamp comparing the two.
knowledge.conditions: Reached in handle_majority_promises after a prepare quorum (leader.rs 257-285) together with set_promise (util.rs 131-149) and get_max_decided_idx (util.rs 168-177); the two orders coincide whenever the promise with the greatest accepted round and index also reports the greatest decided index, which is the case in every observed run of this investigation. knowledge.statement: For a candidate that syncs from the greatest promise, the accepted index it ends with is the adopted promise's own accepted count whenever the resume point lies inside that promise's content: sync_idx is the candidate's decided or accepted index, the suffix is the adopted promise's log from there, and the carried StopSign adds the same one index the adopted promise already counted, so the two accounting terms cancel. Whenever the resume point lies beyond that content the suffix is empty and the candidate ends at sync_idx plus the StopSign term. A disagreement between the adopted decided index and the entries held therefore needs some promise reporting a decided index above the adopted promise's content.
knowledge.conditions: Follows from the two branches of the follower's Promise (common_prefix = prep.decided_idx when na > prep.n_accepted, prep.accepted_idx when equal and greater) and sync_log's accepted accounting; the adopted promise is the strictly greatest under (n_accepted, accepted_idx). knowledge.statement: Repeated re-synchronizations of replicas that already hold the StopSign make the cluster's reported accepted index drift one further index per round while the log content stays fixed, and while the drifting reporters hold a write quorum the leader keeps adopting the maximum reported accepted index as its decided index: over eight further rounds both followers went from accepted 6 / decided 6 to accepted 14 / decided 14 while the leader's own accepted index stayed 6, its decided index followed to 14 and its decided-log read returned nothing in every round. knowledge.statement: With the snapshot-capable entry type, a replica whose reported accepted index lies below the leader's compacted index is re-synchronized without error but receives a complete snapshot built from the entries above its resume point and no suffix: create_log_sync takes its snapshot branch, create_diff_snapshot returns a Complete snapshot with the compacted index the leader currently holds, and the receiving replica installs that snapshot, sets its compacted index to it and reports an accepted index one past it. Where the leader's log held nothing above the compacted index, the installed snapshot is empty, so the replica presented as holding the decided log in fact holds an empty snapshot, its decided-log read drops from the six decided entries to the snapshot entry plus the StopSign, and the same exchange moves the leader's decided index up to the replica's reported (drifted) accepted index.
knowledge.conditions: Snapshot-capable entry type (Snapshot::use_snapshots() true) and a leader whose compacted index exceeds a live replica's reported accepted index, reached after three re-synchronization rounds plus a leader change onto an inflated follower and a local snapshot inside the drifted decided index. Observed in receipt 0b9c22ae5fb043588aa7efa3ad009b25: before the compaction the nodes reported accepted 9 / decided 9, accepted 10 / decided 9 and accepted 9 / decided 9 with decided-log reads of 1, 0 and 2 entries (events 152-154); the snapshot completed with panicked false, compacted index 8, accepted 9, decided 9 and a snapshot holding zero ids (event 155); the re-synchronization of the replica with the lower reported index then left it at accepted 10 / decided 10 with a decided-log read of two entries (event 161) and moved the leader to decided 10 (event 159). No panic was raised (events 162, 166).

interpretations.rationale: Source reading of the re-synchronization path (PrepareReq -> Prepare -> Promise -> AcceptSync -> Accepted) suggests that a replica which has accepted the StopSign gets its accepted index inflated by one when it is re-synchronized at the same ballot: in handle_promise_accept the leader calls send_accsync, whose first branch uses the follower's own accepted index as the valid prefix (leader.rs 150-191), and that index already includes the StopSign because set_stopsign adds it (internal_storage.rs 503-512). create_log_sync then reports that index as LogSync.sync_idx with the sender's StopSign attached, and sync_log adds the StopSign once more, so the follower's accepted index ends at prefix + suffix + 1 while its decided index is the AcceptSync's decided index (internal_storage.rs 313-360). The follower then reports that inflated index in Accepted (follower.rs 112-126), and the leader's decision rule accepts any incoming accepted index whose count reaches a write quorum (leader.rs 316-345), so a write quorum of inflated reports would set the leader's decided index past the entries it holds. Both endpoints this reading endangers are public: is_reconfigured() is gated on stopsign_is_decided() (mod.rs 284-290, state_cache.rs 123-126), the bool of LogEntry::StopSign is documented as 'the reconfiguration has been decided' (util.rs 277-279), and the documented user flow reads the decided suffix and switches configuration only on StopSign(.., true) (reconfiguration.md 25-34). The final judgment is left unresolved until the two-case execution samples the endpoints; the reading also predicts that a fresh or lagging follower, whose prefix does not yet contain the StopSign, is unaffected. Counterevidence and limits: the reconfiguration documentation tells the user to start a new instance once the StopSign is observed as decided, so the affected window is an old instance that keeps running after (or while) it observes the decision and then re-synchronizes; the accounting is correct whenever sync_idx stays at or below the StopSign's own index, which covers the normal catch-up path; the account rests on static reading of the read() combination paths and of MemoryStorage's empty-range behaviour, not on an executed observation.

Confirmed by execution: the re-synchronization of a replica that already accepted its configuration's StopSign inflates its reported accepted index by one, and a write quorum of such reports makes the leader decide an index past every entry it holds. Receipt 8b314551f1e049fcbf73a358f8ddf2c8, two cases in one run over three real OmniPaxos instances with MemoryStorage (events: 19,20,21 = after the StopSign was decided on all three nodes; 22,23 = the two re-synchronized followers; 24 = the leader; 9,10,11 = the identical prefix without reconnected()). Before the re-synchronization all three nodes reported accepted 6, decided 6, is_reconfigured true, read(5) = StopSign with decided = true, and read_decided_suffix(0) = six elements. After both followers called reconnected(3): node 1 and node 2 reported accepted 7 over the same six indices of content, their read(5) returned None (the StopSign is now placed at index 6 by the internal index-type rule), and their decided-log read from 0 returned a single element (the StopSign), so the five decided entries disappeared from the readable decided log while is_reconfigured stayed true; node 3 (leader) reported decided 7 with accepted 6, is_reconfigured false where it had been true, read(5) = StopSign with decided = false, and read_decided_suffix(0) = None, i.e. the user on the leader can no longer read the decided log at all and never observes the reconfiguration as complete. The declared comparisons match this reading: comparison 2 (leader reports the reconfiguration as decided) violated at index 24, comparison 3 (decided index covered by entries held) violated at index 24, comparison 4 (leader's decided log readable from 0) violated at index 24, comparison 5 (re-synchronized follower's decided log still has the five entries plus the StopSign) violated at indices 22 and 23, while comparisons 0 and 1 (the same predicates before the reconnection, indices 19-21) and comparisons 6 and 7 (the no-reconnect control, indices 9-11) hold, which attributes the change to the re-synchronization rather than to the reconfiguration or to the sampling.

27bf7fc0875c4342966bd3dc15df80ec-gap-0.explanation: The legitimate producer path was observed end to end: node 1 and node 2 each called the public reconnected(3) after the StopSign had been accepted and decided; reconnected() sets the follower to Phase::Recover and sends PrepareReq with its current promise (agent-source/omnipaxos/src/sequence_paxos/mod.rs 343-357); the leader in Phase::Accept handles it via handle_preparereq, resets the follower's promise state and re-sends Prepare (leader.rs 66-74); the follower, now in Phase::Recover with its promise equal to the Prepare's ballot, re-promises with accepted_idx = 6, an index that already counts its stored StopSign (follower.rs 13-51, internal_storage.rs 503-512); handle_promise_accept then calls send_accsync (leader.rs 301-314), and because the promise's accepted round equals the leader's current ballot, send_accsync takes its first branch and uses the follower's own accepted index as the valid prefix (leader.rs 150-191), producing LogSync{sync_idx: 6, suffix: [], stopsign: Some} from create_log_sync (mod.rs 405-432); sync_log then adds the StopSign once more (internal_storage.rs 313-360). Receipt 8b314551f1e049fcbf73a358f8ddf2c8 confirms the outcome on the sampled endpoints (events 22 and 23).

counterevidence: The no-reconnect control case of the same execution kept every endpoint consistent (accepted 6, decided 6, is_reconfigured true, six-element decided read at indices 9-11), so the deviation is attributable to the re-established-connection path and not to the reconfiguration, to the harness, or to reading the log.

The documented user flow for reconfiguration (agent-source/docs/omnipaxos/reconfiguration.md 25-34) expects the user to start a new instance once a node observes LogEntry::StopSign(ss, true); a user who stops the old instance immediately limits the user-facing window, but does not remove the defect: the leader of the same run never observes the StopSign as decided after the corruption (is_reconfigured false, decided log unreadable), and the two followers keep reporting the reconfiguration as decided while their decided log silently loses the five decided entries.

The leader's phantom decision is inferred from its own reported state (decided 7 with accepted 6 and six indices of content) plus the two followers' inflated 7; the internal accepted-index vector was not sampled, so the assignment of which reports formed the quorum rests on the source rule (handle_accepted decides any incoming accepted index reaching a write quorum) rather than on a direct trace of that vector.
limitations: No snapshots (NoSnapshot entries) and default batch size 1: whether the snapshot-enabled branch of create_log_sync inflates the same way is untested.

Messages were delivered in FIFO order without loss and without tick()-driven timers, so the re-established-connection call is the only recovery trigger exercised; loss-triggered re-synchronization is untested.

All three nodes used in-memory storage; persistence across a restart and the behaviour of other storages on out-of-range reads (a storage-implementer responsibility per the Storage trait) were not exercised.

The re-synchronization needed two followers of a three-node cluster to inflate for the leader to decide the phantom index 7; the single-replica case is targeted by the successor experiment submitted with this update.

interpretations.rationale: The isolating successor run confirms and narrows the account. Receipt 9125b6a531234e7d9d2fa8cbb817df63 (same harness lineage, third case added; all three tests passed) showed: with only node 1 re-synchronized, node 1 alone ended at accepted 7 over the same six indices of content, decided 6, so its own reported reconfiguration endpoint flipped from true to false, its read of the StopSign's index 5 returned None while its read of index 6 returned the StopSign, and its decided-log read from 0 returned an empty list where it had returned six elements before (event 35); nodes 2 and 3 stayed at 6/6 with a six-element decided read and is_reconfigured true (events 36, 37). That separates the two consequences: the follower-local inflation and endpoint/read corruption need only one re-synchronized replica, while the leader's decision at index 7 requires a write quorum of inflated reports (the two-follower case, event 24 in both receipts). The comparisons match: on the single case, comparisons 3-6 (node 1 reports the reconfiguration as decided; its decided index is covered by the entries it holds; its StopSign stays at index 5; its decided log keeps six elements) were violated at index 35, while comparisons 7-8 (the leader still reports the reconfiguration as decided and stays consistent) hold at index 37; comparison 2 holds the baseline that index 6 held no StopSign before the re-synchronization (index 19). The declared defect stands: a public reconnected() call on a replica that has accepted the configuration's StopSign corrupts that replica's index accounting, hides the configuration transition from the user, and - with a write quorum of such reports - makes the leader declare a decided index past every entry it holds, after which the leader itself no longer reports the reconfiguration as decided and cannot read its decided log at all.

counterevidence: The no-reconnect control of the same execution kept every endpoint consistent (accepted 6, decided 6, is_reconfigured true, six-element decided read; receipt 8b314551f1e049fcbf73a358f8ddf2c8 events 9-11 and the control case of the successor run), so the deviation is caused by the re-established-connection path rather than by the reconfiguration, the harness or the reading.

The single-replica case limits the leader-side consequence: one inflated report did not reach a write quorum, so the leader kept decided 6 with is_reconfigured true (receipt 9125b6a531234e7d9d2fa8cbb817df63 event 37); the decision at the phantom index therefore requires a write quorum of inflated reports (both followers of a three-node cluster) within one term.

The documented reconfiguration flow (agent-source/docs/omnipaxos/reconfiguration.md 25-34) expects the user to start a new instance once a node observes LogEntry::StopSign(ss, true), so a user who stops the old instance immediately narrows the user-facing window; the defect still bites the leader, which never observes the decision after the corruption, and any replica whose log is read while its old instance still runs.

The leader's phantom decision is inferred from its reported state (decided 7 with accepted 6 and six indices of content) plus the followers' inflated 7; the internal accepted-index vector was not sampled, so which reports formed the quorum rests on the source rule that any matching-ballot Accepted index counts, not on a direct trace.
limitations: No snapshot-enabled execution has been run; the sourced applicability fact says the snapshot branch computes sync_idx without the StopSign, so the defect is not specific to NoSnapshot entries, but that branch was not exercised.

Messages were delivered in FIFO order without loss and without tick()-driven timers, so the re-established-connection call is the only recovery trigger exercised; a loss-triggered re-synchronization path that produces the same resume point is untested.

The consequence is bounded by the sealed configuration: after the StopSign is accepted no further entries can be accepted, so the phantom decided index carries no value and no value can be mis-assigned; the demonstrated effects are the corrupted index accounting, the unreadable or blank decided log, and the lost reconfiguration endpoint rather than divergent values.

interpretations.rationale: Source trace only, no execution. handle_majority_promises pairs two independently ordered inputs: the log_sync of the promise that is strictly greatest under (n_accepted, accepted_idx) (set_promise only replaces max_promise_meta on a strict Greater, and PromiseMetaData's ordering ignores decided_idx) and the maximum decided_idx across all recorded promises (get_max_decided_idx). sync_log then stores the adopted decided index together with the adopted log and does not clamp. Because the decided index adopted is a different node's report, a history in which the greatest-accepted promise holds fewer entries than another promise's reported decided index would leave the new leader reporting a decided index beyond the entries it holds; every observed run so far has the two orders coincide (the greatest-accepted promise was also the greatest decided reporter), so no witness exists. The suspicion is therefore unresolved rather than refuted: the reachability argument I can give (a decided entry must be accepted by a write quorum that intersects every read quorum, so the greatest-accepted promise should cover it) is exactly the protocol invariant that this code relies on instead of a local bound, and I have not turned it into a reachable disagreement history.

interpretations.rationale: Source trace plus a narrowing argument, still without an execution. handle_majority_promises pairs two independently ordered inputs: the log from the promise that is strictly greatest under (n_accepted, accepted_idx) (set_promise replaces max_promise_meta only on a strict Greater; PromiseMetaData's ordering ignores decided_idx) and the decided index from the greatest decided_idx over all recorded promises (get_max_decided_idx); sync_log stores both without clamping, and the leader path has no counterpart to the follower's update_decided_idx_and_get_accepted_idx. For the pairing to break the adopted decided index must exceed the entries the adopted log provides, which requires a promise whose reported decided_idx is greater than the content the leader ends up holding. Narrowing: in the configurations examined here the interposing +1 for a carried StopSign keeps the adopted accepted index at or above the adopted decided index whenever the greatest-accepted promise is the one holding the decided prefix - in the resync/newterm/staleleader runs the followers reported decided 7 with content 6 and the greatest-accepted promise was exactly such a replica, so the leader's post-sync accepted index (sync_idx + suffix + 1) came out at 7 as well and the two matched. A disagreement therefore needs a promise reporting a decided index above its own content while not being the greatest-accepted promise, which none of the observed anomalies produced for the adopted maximum. The suspicion stays unresolved rather than refuted: the protocol argument (a decided entry is accepted by a write quorum intersecting every read quorum, so the greatest-accepted promise should already cover it) is exactly what this code relies on instead of a local bound, and I have neither constructed a reachable disagreement nor bounded it with an execution.

counterevidence: The two orderings coincide in every observed run of this investigation, so no observation supports a disagreement yet.
limitations: No execution: the account rests on reading handle_majority_promises, set_promise, get_max_decided_idx and sync_log.

Larger clusters, where a promise reporting a high no-StopSign decided index could coexist with a greater-accepted, shorter promise, are untested.

interpretations.rationale: Refuted as an independent defect by source arithmetic, with the residual dependence stated. The candidate's accepted index after the prepare phase is determined by the adopted promise: with the resume point inside that promise's content the candidate ends at exactly the adopted promise's accepted count, because the suffix supplies the entries from the resume point to that content and the carried StopSign adds the same one index the adopted promise had already counted (the follower's Promise sets common_prefix to the candidate's decided index when its accepted round is higher, and to the candidate's accepted index when the rounds are equal and it is further ahead); with the resume point beyond that content the suffix is empty and the candidate ends at the resume point plus the StopSign term. In both cases the candidate's accepted index is at least the adopted promise's content, so for the adopted decided index to exceed the entries held some promise must report a decided index above the adopted promise's content. For truthful reports that is excluded by the protocol's own invariant that a promise with a higher accepted round covers everything decided - the property this code relies on instead of a local clamp - and for corrupted reports the only producers observed in this investigation are the inflated accepted indexes already covered by the parent question, which also leave the adopted decided index equal to or below the leader's accepted index in the newterm and staleleader stages. The two orderings coincided in every observed run, and no run produced a decided index above the adopted log's content, so the suspicion is refuted in its independent form while the residual case (a legal history in which the greatest-accepted promise is not the greatest decided reporter and the invariant fails) remains only as a consequence of the parent's corruption.

The same effect appeared for a follower re-promising in an ordinary new term (6cdcff36336646859bffb9e8c3e39789 event 11), for the leader that took over from such a follower (dda5bb4179154e3abe90e69f5267b3ea event 13) and under a snapshot-capable entry type (fd0b8be59c8f466fbf7768abb08f93b5 events 51, 52). No bound on the drift was observed inside the sealed configuration; the run stopped after three rounds by construction.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only account of a lead, with an explicit argument for why it is not yet settled. trim takes its bound from the minimum of the recorded accepted indexes (util.rs 186-191) and compares the requested index against it (mod.rs 141-170), while the documented contract for trimming requires all nodes to have decided the trim index (compaction.md line 4); the parent question witnesses that those recorded indexes can exceed a replica's content by one per re-synchronization, so the minimum trim trusts is not necessarily a decided bound. The narrow counter-argument that keeps this unresolved rather than asserted: in the observed single-term drift the leading node's own recorded accepted index stayed at its content (6), so the minimum stayed truthful, and the trim bound is further adjusted by the StopSign (try_trim maps an index equal to the decided index to the decided log without the StopSign), which in the observed states cancelled the drift exactly. An over-trim therefore needs a state in which every recorded accepted index exceeds the entries its node holds, which the witnessed staleleader stage comes close to but was not sampled at a trim; the storage-side consequence I can source is that MemoryStorage computes suffix reads and prefix truncations by subtracting its compacted index (memory_storage.rs 64-67, 92-107, 122-127), so a compacted index above the requested prefix would underflow there.
counterevidence: In the observed drift the leading node's recorded accepted index stayed at its content, so the minimum trim uses was still truthful.
try_trim adjusts an index equal to the decided index to the decided log without the StopSign, which cancelled the observed drift instead of over-trimming.
limitations: No execution: trim after a drift was not exercised, and no observed state had every node's recorded accepted index above its content at the moment of a trim.
The underflow hypothesis rests on reading MemoryStorage's arithmetic; other storages may behave differently and the trait leaves out-of-range behaviour to the implementer.
The drift itself was exercised for three rounds only.

interpretations.rationale: Witnessed: the drifted accepted indexes reach the trim bound, and trim acts on it. Receipt ec3329dc273e452aa92bcd44652c116a: after three reconnection rounds and a leader change, the leader held six indices of content (five entries plus the StopSign) while the recorded accepted indexes were 10, 9 and 7 and every node's decided report had drifted to 9 (events 9-11); the public trim(None) then returned no error and compacted index 7 (event 12), i.e. more indices than the log contains and more than the five entry indices, and the leader's subsequent reads of indices 5 and 6 reported Trimmed with a two-element decided-log read (event 14) while both followers still reported accepted 10 and 7 with decided 9 (events 13, 15). The declared comparison requiring the compacted index to reach the six decided indices was violated at that event, and the comparison requiring trim to succeed was recorded unknown only because its admission chain was built on an event name shared with another case in the same execution; the sampled operands show the call returned Ok. The mechanism is the child question's premise: trim derives its bound from the minimum recorded accepted index (util.rs 186-191) and compares it against the leader's decided index (mod.rs 141-170) rather than against what each replica holds, so once the drift lifts those recorded values the leader's own content no longer bounds the compaction. The documented requirement that all nodes have decided the trim index is met only in the same drifted bookkeeping (their decided reports are drifted too), which is why I keep the counterevidence explicit rather than treating the documentation as the violated duty; the duty that fails on admissible input is that the trim bound must not exceed the entries the leader itself holds, and it does here.
counterevidence: Every node's decided report had also drifted to 9, so the documented precondition (all nodes decided the trim index) was satisfied in the drifted bookkeeping; the violated obligation I rely on is instead that the compacted index must stay within the content the leader holds, which it did not (7 against 6 indices).
The trim call itself returned Ok, so nothing in the call's own result signals the over-compaction; the witness is the compacted index together with the content sampled before and after.
limitations: The downstream hazard I sourced (a later suffix request below the compacted index underflowing MemoryStorage's arithmetic) was not triggered: no promise or log-sync in this run asked for a prefix below the compacted index, so the over-compaction is witnessed with reads and the compacted index, not with a crash.

The drift and therefore the over-compaction were produced with three reconnection rounds and one leader change in a three-node cluster; other sizes, rounds and producers were not exercised.
No snapshot was created, so after the trim the entries were simply removed; whether a snapshot-enabled configuration would instead compact into a snapshot that no replica can serve was not exercised.

interpretations.rationale: Witnessed and then narrowed. Receipt ec3329dc273e452aa92bcd44652c116a: with the recorded accepted indexes drifted to 10, 9 and 7 over six indices of content (five entries plus the StopSign) and every node's decided report drifted to 9, the public trim(None) returned no error and compacted index 7 - past the leader's own content - after which the leader's reads of indices 5 and 6 reported Trimmed with a two-element decided-log read (event 14) while the followers still reported accepted 10 and 7 (events 13, 15); the declared comparison requiring the compacted index to reach the six decided indices was violated at the trim event. Narrowing of the consequence, from reading the same derivation: both trim paths are bounded by the minimum recorded accepted index (the explicit-index path refuses any index above it and reports that minimum), so a trim can never compact past the content of a replica whose recorded accepted index is truthful - such a replica would itself supply a lower minimum. That bounds the over-compaction to exceeding the content of replicas whose own recorded values have drifted, which is exactly the witnessed leader, and it also removes the crash path I had sourced from the same lead: a suffix or log-sync request below the compacted index could only come from a replica whose recorded value is below it, and in the drifted cluster every node's recorded value is at or above the compacted index (the trim bound equals the minimum recorded value), so no request in this configuration can reach the arithmetic that would underflow. The hazard therefore stays a sourced possibility for a store or caller that asks below the compacted index by another route, not a consequence of this witness.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only lead, opened because it is a different producer from the trim path that already produced a witnessed over-compaction. try_snapshot compares a user-supplied index against the leader's decided index (internal_storage.rs 432-453), and the documented note in the same function's caller states what may be snapshotted (mod.rs 180-184); the witnessed drift lifts that decided index above the content, so the comparison no longer keeps the request inside the entries a replica holds. create_snapshot then builds the snapshot from the storage range starting at the current compacted index (internal_storage.rs 367-383), and the in-memory storage returns an empty vector when the range does not exist (memory_storage.rs 92-107), so a request whose range lies past the entries would store a snapshot created from nothing while advancing the compacted index. What keeps this unresolved rather than asserted: the drift in the observed runs was produced with the same sealed configuration and a StopSign, where try_snapshot's equal case maps the decided index to the decided log without the StopSign, which lowered the effective bound in the states I sampled; and no snapshot call has been executed after a drift, so neither the acceptance of such a request nor what a reader then sees has been observed.

interpretations.rationale: Witnessed: the snapshot path compacts and snapshots past the entries the leader holds, and the snapshot it produces holds none of them. Receipt e70b8baa087246c78ea3a64f24b8e97c: after the drift the three nodes reported accepted 9, 9 and 6 with decided 9 while the leader held six indices of content (events 0-2); the public snapshot(Some(8), false) returned Ok, the leader's compacted index became 8, its accepted index stayed 6 and its decided index 9, and the snapshot served for index 0 held zero entry ids where the log had five decided entries (event 3). The declared comparisons requiring the compacted index to stay at the six indices of content and the snapshot to hold the five entries were both violated at that event, and the comparison requiring the call to be accepted was recorded unknown only because its admission chain shared an event name with another case in the same execution, while the operand shows the call returned Ok. Mechanism: try_snapshot bounds the request by the leader's decided index (internal_storage.rs 432-453) and the documented note permits exactly that (mod.rs 180-184), while create_snapshot builds the snapshot from the range starting at the current compacted index (internal_storage.rs 367-383); the drift lifts the decided index above the content, and the in-memory storage returns nothing for a range that does not exist (memory_storage.rs 92-107), so the snapshot is built from an empty slice while the compacted index passes the entries. The entries are no longer reachable through the log and the snapshot that now represents them is empty, which for an application that keeps its state in the snapshot means the state it compacted away is silently gone; the trigger is a caller-visible index the documentation describes as allowed, so the responsibility sits with the target's bound and range derivation rather than with the caller.

interpretations.rationale: The public snapshot() path reaches a panicking constructor on the crate's own placeholder snapshot type, and it does so on any instance of that type, not only on a drifted one. SequencePaxos::snapshot forwards the caller's index to InternalStorage::try_snapshot, which resolves the bound through the decided index and then, whenever that bound exceeds the current compacted index, calls create_snapshot and hence T::Snapshot::create; nothing on the path consults T::Snapshot::use_snapshots(), and for T::Snapshot = NoSnapshot that body is panic!("NoSnapshot should not be created"). The documentation for snapshot() bounds the index only by the decided index, and the Entry trait lets a configuration name NoSnapshot as its placeholder for not using snapshots, so no caller-side marker distinguishes the call as invalid. Witness on a healthy cluster: all three nodes reported accepted 6 / decided 6 with is_reconfigured true and a readable six-element decided log (receipt 0b9c22ae5fb043588aa7efa3ad009b25 events 238-240), and snapshot(Some(6), true) on the leader panicked with panicked true, the compacted index still 0 and accepted and decided still 6 (event 241), the process naming omnipaxos/src/storage/mod.rs:205 and NoSnapshot should not be created; the three nodes were still consistent afterwards (events 242-244). Witness on a drifted instance: the same call with the drifted decided bound on a leader reporting accepted 9 / decided 9 panicked in the same way (receipt 2cb2a3f1e43b4942b5bb3f42bad11091 event 129). Because both witnesses raise the panic before any storage write, the failure mode is an aborted caller with no state change and no error return; the same snapshot entry is used by the compaction-forwarding handler, so a forwarded Snapshot compaction arriving at such an instance would unwind inside message handling, which remains a source-level consequence because no execution produced such a message.
counterevidence: The crate documents NoSnapshot as a placeholder for configurations that do not use snapshots and implements create and merge as panicking stubs, so the panic is that type's declared behaviour when invoked; the deviation is that the documented public path invokes it instead of refusing or erroring, and the caller receives no CompactionErr.

The call is a user-initiated snapshot request, so a caller that knows its entry type cannot use snapshots could avoid it; the defect is the abort rather than a silent wrong result, and no data is lost because the unwind happens before the storage write (compacted index 0 and unchanged indices in both witnesses).
The drift is not required: the healthy control shows the same panic with a consistent six-entry decided log, so this account does not depend on the parent investigation's index accounting.
limitations: Only one entry type was used for the witnesses (the harness's Value with Snapshot = NoSnapshot); whether a derive-macro-generated Snapshot type defaults to NoSnapshot and therefore inherits the panic was not established.

No forwarded Compaction::Snapshot message was ever delivered to such an instance, because one cluster in this harness uses one entry type and the leader that would send it panics first, so the handler-side abort is argued from source.

The lagging-replica loss of class (6) requires a snapshot-capable entry type whose snapshot can be built from an empty range; the non-snapshot variant of the same probe could not be executed at all, because snapshot() panics on that type for reasons independent of the drift (recorded under 40ab66a5c5c847619ae2ff68b85641e7-question-1).

The last executed state is not evidence of a limit: the decided index stopped following only because the reports outran a write quorum in that term, and no execution varied the number of replicas or the number of drifting reporters to see how that boundary moves.
limitations: The drift was exercised for eleven rounds with one mid-run leader change; that range found no bound and no repair, but the decided index stopped following once the reports outran every write quorum, so how far the decided index can keep following is a quorum property that was observed with one three-node pattern rather than characterised in general.
Loss-triggered and timer-triggered re-synchronization were not exercised; the producers observed are explicit reconnected() calls and an ordinary leader change onto a node that had already drifted.

Only three-node clusters were used, with in-memory storage, no persistence across restarts and one snapshot-capable entry type; the compaction witnesses depend on that entry type's snapshot semantics, and the entry type that cannot carry a snapshot aborts the compaction call instead of losing entries.

Several comparisons across the repeated-rounds, trim, snapshot, drift-bound and over-compaction receipts came out unknown because their admissions shared event names across cases in one execution or put a node condition on the prerequisite; those states are asserted from the sampled operands, with the violated comparisons cited above.

The cases sample after each drained round, so they do not show intermediate states inside a round, and no case exercised the forwarded compaction messages that a snapshot or trim call with local_only = false would send to peers; the peer-side variant is therefore argued from the per-node derivation of the bound and the range, not sampled.

The lagging-replica loss was observed once, with the leader's log empty above the compacted index, so whether a non-empty remainder would be handed over instead of an empty snapshot is not established; the receipt's own snapshot held zero ids.

The consequence set stays within index accounting, readability and compaction; the sealed configuration admits no further entries and refuses appends while the StopSign is stored, so no value is mis-assigned.

The routes by which a storage or caller could ask for a prefix below a compacted index by another entry point (a direct range read, a store-level trim, a peer whose recorded values were truthful) remain unexecuted, as recorded in the trim child's open gap.

result.summary: Closed the remaining in-cluster half of the audit's last open gap by reading the leader's recorded-accepted bookkeeping, and recorded the split so only the storage-level entry point stays open. LeaderState::get_min_all_accepted_idx is the minimum over the accepted_indexes vector, and the source asserts that vector is initialised for every node (its expect message reads Should be all initialised to 0) while set_promise rewrites the sender's entry on every promise; a truthful replica therefore keeps its own accepted index inside the minimum, so trim cannot pass it and no re-synchronization request below a trim-produced compacted index can arise inside the cluster. That closes, by source, the sub-route the trim child's gap named as a peer compacted while its recorded values were still truthful, and it joins the executed half already recorded: a replica re-synchronized below a compacted index is not refused and does not abort, it receives a complete snapshot built from the empty part of the log and a shortened decided log (receipt 0b9c22ae5fb043588aa7efa3ad009b25 events 152-162, guarded result event 162 with panicked false), while the abort this lineage did produce belongs to the public snapshot call on a NoSnapshot instance and stays under its own question. The trim child's account was rewritten as a successor with that split in its own answers, its counterevidence and limitations now distinguishing what is executed, what is closed by source, and what is untested, and the trim-bound fact was revised so its conditions carry the initialisation basis rather than the observed drift alone. No execution was requested and nothing was run, so the remaining work is explicitly left as work: the storage-level routes a caller could use below a compacted index (a direct range read, a store-level trim), the forwarded-compaction and peer-sampling variants, the delivery of a forwarded Compaction::Snapshot to a NoSnapshot instance, and the bookkeeping detail that the revised trim-bound fact's affected uses were not enumerated in the same update.

knowledge.statement: InternalStorage::sync_log sets accepted_idx = LogSync.sync_idx + LogSync.suffix.len() and, when LogSync.stopsign is Some, adds one further index for that StopSign before returning; it does not subtract the LogSync's prefix, so when sync_idx already addresses the StopSign's own index the replica's accepted index ends up one larger than the entries it holds, and each further re-synchronization of the same replica adds one more index while its content is unchanged. knowledge.statement: A leader in the accept phase accepts a decision at the accepted index reported by any matching-ballot Accepted message: it records that index for the sender, and if the index exceeds its own decided index and a write quorum of recorded accepted indexes covers it, it sets its decided index to exactly that reported index, without comparing it against the length of its own log or against its own accepted index.
knowledge.conditions: Leader role in Phase::Accept with a matching ballot; the recorded accepted indexes include the leader's own slot as it was last written by its own accept handling. knowledge.statement: When a candidate becomes leader it adopts two independently ordered inputs in one call: the log comes from the promise that is strictly greatest under (n_accepted, accepted_idx) with pid only as tiebreak, while the decided index is the maximum decided index over all recorded promises; sync_log then writes that decided index and the adopted log in the same storage transaction, and the leader path contains no clamp comparing the two.
knowledge.conditions: Reached in handle_majority_promises after a prepare quorum (leader.rs 257-285) together with set_promise (util.rs 131-149) and get_max_decided_idx (util.rs 168-177); the two orders coincide whenever the promise with the greatest accepted round and index also reports the greatest decided index, which is the case in every observed run of this investigation. Sourced only; no execution has yet produced a disagreement between the two orders.

knowledge.statement: For a candidate that syncs from the greatest promise, the accepted index it ends with is the adopted promise's own accepted count whenever the resume point lies inside that promise's content: sync_idx is the candidate's decided or accepted index, the suffix is the adopted promise's log from there, and the carried StopSign adds the same one index the adopted promise already counted, so the two accounting terms cancel. Whenever the resume point lies beyond that content the suffix is empty and the candidate ends at sync_idx plus the StopSign term. A disagreement between the adopted decided index and the entries held therefore needs some promise reporting a decided index above the adopted promise's content.
knowledge.conditions: Follows from the two branches of the follower's Promise (common_prefix = prep.decided_idx when na > prep.n_accepted, prep.accepted_idx when equal and greater) and sync_log's accepted accounting; the adopted promise is the strictly greatest under (n_accepted, accepted_idx). Sourced; the three-node runs of this investigation had the greatest promise also reporting the greatest decided index, so the disagreement never arose there.

knowledge.statement: Repeated re-synchronizations of replicas that already hold the StopSign make the cluster's reported accepted index drift one further index per round while the log content stays fixed, and while the drifting reporters hold a write quorum the leader keeps adopting the maximum reported accepted index as its decided index: over eight further rounds both followers went from accepted 6 / decided 6 to accepted 14 / decided 14 while the leader's own accepted index stayed 6, its decided index followed to 14 and its decided-log read returned nothing in every round. The drift neither saturates nor is repaired inside the sealed configuration: a leader change onto one of the inflated followers left that node at accepted 14 instead of re-deriving its six indices of content, the previously truthful replica was itself re-synchronized to accepted 7, and in the three following rounds the followers' accepted indexes rose to 18 and 10 while the decided index froze at 14 because no write quorum of recorded accepted indexes covered the further reports.
knowledge.conditions: Three-node cluster after a decided StopSign, each round being a pair of public reconnected() calls addressing the current leader, with nothing else proposed. Observed over three rounds in receipt 6c879304cdde4ddd8e1640207cdbf94d (followers 7 then 8 then 9 at events 41, 42, 44, 45, 47, 48; leader decided 7 then 8 then 9 with accepted 6 at events 43, 46, 49) and over eight rounds plus a leader change plus three further rounds in receipt 2993c16874454f86a3f8b04364a00ef4 (baseline accepted 6 / decided 6 events 9-11; followers accepted 7 at events 12, 13 and 14 at events 33, 34; leader accepted 6 with decided 7 and 14 and an unreadable decided log at events 14, 20, 35; after the leader change node 1 at accepted 14 / decided 14, node 2 at accepted 15, node 3 at accepted 7, events 36-38; last round node 2 at accepted 18 and node 3 at accepted 10 with decided 14, events 46, 47; eleven guarded stages with zero panics, event 48). interpretations.rationale: Source reading of the re-synchronization path (PrepareReq -> Prepare -> Promise -> AcceptSync -> Accepted) suggests that a replica which has accepted the StopSign gets its accepted index inflated by one when it is re-synchronized at the same ballot: in handle_promise_accept the leader calls send_accsync, whose first branch uses the follower's own accepted index as the valid prefix (leader.rs 150-191), and that index already includes the StopSign because set_stopsign adds it (internal_storage.rs 503-512). create_log_sync then reports that index as LogSync.sync_idx with the sender's StopSign attached, and sync_log adds the StopSign once more, so the follower's accepted index ends at prefix + suffix + 1 while its decided index is the AcceptSync's decided index (internal_storage.rs 313-360). The follower then reports that inflated index in Accepted (follower.rs 112-126), and the leader's decision rule accepts any incoming accepted index whose count reaches a write quorum (leader.rs 316-345), so a write quorum of inflated reports would set the leader's decided index past the entries it holds. Both endpoints this reading endangers are public: is_reconfigured() is gated on stopsign_is_decided() (mod.rs 284-290, state_cache.rs 123-126), the bool of LogEntry::StopSign is documented as 'the reconfiguration has been decided' (util.rs 277-279), and the documented user flow reads the decided suffix and switches configuration only on StopSign(.., true) (reconfiguration.md 25-34). The final judgment is left unresolved until the two-case execution samples the endpoints; the reading also predicts that a fresh or lagging follower, whose prefix does not yet contain the StopSign, is unaffected. Counterevidence and limits: the reconfiguration documentation tells the user to start a new instance once the StopSign is observed as decided, so the affected window is an old instance that keeps running after (or while) it observes the decision and then re-synchronizes; the accounting is correct whenever sync_idx stays at or below the StopSign's own index, which covers the normal catch-up path; the account rests on static reading of the read() combination paths and of MemoryStorage's empty-range behaviour, not on an executed observation.

Confirmed by execution: the re-synchronization of a replica that already accepted its configuration's StopSign inflates its reported accepted index by one, and a write quorum of such reports makes the leader decide an index past every entry it holds. Receipt 8b314551f1e049fcbf73a358f8ddf2c8, two cases in one run over three real OmniPaxos instances with MemoryStorage (events: 19,20,21 = after the StopSign was decided on all three nodes; 22,23 = the two re-synchronized followers; 24 = the leader; 9,10,11 = the identical prefix without reconnected()). Before the re-synchronization all three nodes reported accepted 6, decided 6, is_reconfigured true, read(5) = StopSign with decided = true, and read_decided_suffix(0) = six elements. After both followers called reconnected(3): node 1 and node 2 reported accepted 7 over the same six indices of content, their read(5) returned None (the StopSign is now placed at index 6 by the internal index-type rule), and their decided-log read from 0 returned a single element (the StopSign), so the five decided entries disappeared from the readable decided log while is_reconfigured stayed true; node 3 (leader) reported decided 7 with accepted 6, is_reconfigured false where it had been true, read(5) = StopSign with decided = false, and read_decided_suffix(0) = None, i.e. the user on the leader can no longer read the decided log at all and never observes the reconfiguration as complete. The declared comparisons match this reading: comparison 2 (leader reports the reconfiguration as decided) violated at index 24, comparison 3 (decided index covered by entries held) violated at index 24, comparison 4 (leader's decided log readable from 0) violated at index 24, comparison 5 (re-synchronized follower's decided log still has the five entries plus the StopSign) violated at indices 22 and 23, while comparisons 0 and 1 (the same predicates before the reconnection, indices 19-21) and comparisons 6 and 7 (the no-reconnect control, indices 9-11) hold, which attributes the change to the re-synchronization rather than to the reconfiguration or to the sampling.

counterevidence: The crate documents NoSnapshot as a placeholder for configurations that do not use snapshots and implements create and merge as panicking stubs, so the panic is that type's declared behaviour when invoked; the deviation is that the documented public path invokes it instead of refusing or erroring, and the caller receives no CompactionErr.

The call is a user-initiated snapshot request, so a caller that knows its entry type cannot use snapshots could avoid it; the defect is the abort rather than a silent wrong result, and no data is lost because the unwind happens before the storage write (compacted index 0 and unchanged indices in both witnesses).
The drift is not required: the healthy control shows the same panic with a consistent six-entry decided log, so this account does not depend on the parent investigation's index accounting.
limitations: Only one entry type was used for the witnesses (the harness's Value with Snapshot = NoSnapshot); whether a derive-macro-generated Snapshot type defaults to NoSnapshot and therefore inherits the panic was not established.

No forwarded Compaction::Snapshot message was ever delivered to such an instance, because one cluster in this harness uses one entry type and the leader that would send it panics first, so the handler-side abort is argued from source.
The panic is observed through catch_unwind, which reports the abort of the call but not the state a process without the guard would be in; no restart or supervision behaviour was exercised.

limitations: The trim over-compaction is bounded to replicas whose recorded accepted index has drifted; a truthful replica would have kept the bound lower, and the per-node initialisation of the recorded vector is the reason.

The underflow remainder is a property of a storage or caller that requests a prefix below the compacted index by a route other than the cluster's own log syncs: a direct range read and a store-level trim below a compacted index remain unexecuted, other storage implementations may differ, and the trait leaves out-of-range behaviour to the implementer. The abort observed in this lineage came from the NoSnapshot snapshot-call path, not from this remainder.

For the trim path the observed over-compaction is the minimum of the drifted recorded values, so the number of indices it passes beyond the leader's content depends on how many rounds each replica drifted; only one such combination was sampled.
